newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Putting South Africa down - by E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Putting South Africa down - by E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

In an article I wrote last December I predicted a negative GDP growth figure for the fourth quarter of 1996 because of an expected fall back of agriculture from its historical high in the third quarter -- on each previous occasion of attaining such a high level there was a drop back in the succeeding quarter.

In the event agriculture did continue to grow, according to the official estimates, and there was a positive growth of GDP. However, there was a large swing downwards in the first quarter of 1997 which has effected an overall decline in market-prices GDP of 0.8 percent, annualised.
Although agriculture represents only some 6.5 percent of total national output, the extreme fluctuations resulting from changing conditions do have a significant impact on the overall result.

The Central Statistical Service (CSS) is dependent on the Department of Agriculture for the estimates for agriculture. These are carefully and conscientiously made, but the very nature of agricultural activity is such that they do not lend themselves readily to concepts of national accounting on a quarterly basis. It is for this reason that the U.S. produces quarterly GDP figures for the economy excluding agriculture.

Basically the Department relies on crop estimates which, of course, change as the season progresses. Thus, high crop expectations, say in the fourth quarter, will give a high growth figure of the sector's contribution to GDP in that quarter. Should conditions deteriorate with downward adjustments to the crop estimates there will be a downturn in the sector, which should necessitate revisions to the previous quarter or quarters where the same crops are involved.

However, for practical reasons the CSS has a policy of only providing revisions to past estimates mainly in September but occasionally at six month intervals if there are compelling reasons. So here we have had an instance where deteriorating conditions have apparently reduced agriculture's contribution to GDP by 34 percent against an unrevised estimate for the fourth quarter of 1996 when the crop expectations were outstanding and a growth of 12.6 percent annualised, was estimated.
Although we are essentially dealing with the same crops the estimates, as published, reflect the change of expectations. Strictly the CSS should have revised the previous estimates.

The CSS argues that they eventually get their estimates for the year as a whole correct. To them the estimates for the quarters are very rough and ready and purely indicate trends. They are provisional.
However, the public and the markets do not interpret the figures in this way and tend to give too much credence to the finer movements of the estimates from quarter to quarter.

If we can assume that the fourth quarter for agriculture should be revised downwards to an intermediate point between the third quarter of 1996 and the first quarter of 1997, the factor-cost GDP growth for the fourth quarter of 1996 would be revised downwards from 3.1 percent to 1.5 percent, and the first quarter 1997 growth would be increased from minus 1.15 percent to plus 0.4 percent.

The growth of GDP at market prices in the first quarter of 1997 is shifted upwards from minus 0.82 percent to plus 0.58 percent. And, incidentally, the 1996 factor-cost GDP growth of 3.0 percent is pulled down to 2.9 percent.

Clearly we ought to place greater confidence on the non-agricultural GDP figures for impressions of trends. On this basis the estimates for the March quarter of 1997 should not give cause for despondency or expectations of recession.
The annualised growth was 1.36 percent, as compared with 0.63 percent in the corresponding first quarter of 1996, but admittedly down from 2.51 percent in the December 1996 quarter.

But even with these figures there is something of a question mark hanging over the manufacturing estimate for there is a very wide discrepancy between the CSS estimate of manufacturing growth of 3.65 percent and the corresponding growth of the manufacturing output index of 9.51 percent.

Although the basic concepts of value added are common to both, the movements have never corresponded exactly. There is a tendency to have exaggerated fluctuations in the manufacturing index where the indicators are deflated sales figures, which are fairly far removed from actual production levels.

However, the disturbing aspect of the manufacturing index figures is that the overwhelming contribution to growth is confined to petroleum refining and non-ferrous basic metals. In other words we are seeing positive growth in the capital-intensive industries and a relatively static situation in the rest of manufacturing.
This is the truly disturbing conclusion to be drawn from the figures; namely that we are going through structural change in the direction of jobless growth.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
